input.add_to_description: Meeting Tamsin Vale: took her two coppers, let her pole the punt, approved of her hands. Told her the village is Reedholm; that the Wick-fires were quiet for years after the Isle was salted and its gap sealed, but green-white lights returned over the Isle about a month ago; that Wren the healer (wears an old wooden amulet) is the one to ask about the Isle. Pim's grey dog is called Sedge's Dog (unnamed yet).

entries.text:
You tell him what you see in his work, and the wariness goes out of his shoulders a little. "Hands that know rope," he says, taking the two coppers. "Pim Tarr." He nods at the stern pole. "Take her across, then. I'll walk the bank-line and watch how you read the water."

You cast off. The punt is broad and honest and handles like a good one. The channel is slow and black, and the current moves under the hull with a cold, patient weight, the way deep water does when nothing is hurrying it. Pim stands in the bow with the lantern. He says nothing until you are past mid-channel, then grunts. "You'll do."

You ask your question. He stays quiet long enough that the dog, which has followed along the bank, whines once.

"Reedholm," he says. "That's the village. Fen-cutters and eel-trappers, a hundred souls now, where there were sixty." He doesn't look at you. "The Hollow Isle is a mile west of the landing. There's a grey stone fallen there, and the gap in its flank was sealed with stone and salt the year the old healer died. The lights went quiet after that and stayed quiet for years." He turns the lantern a little. "A month ago they came back. Pale green-white, low over the water. Nobody speaks of it much. If you want to hear it properly, ask Wren. She keeps the Long House and the healing. She wears an old wooden amulet from a man who died out there, and she has opinions about strangers, so mind your tongue."

The far bank rises out of the dusk, a reed-wall with a plank landing, and the yellow window-lights are closer now. A bell on a post stands at the landing, silent. The drizzle has stopped, and a mist is coming up off the water, low and slow.

It's six o'clock on Day 1 of this new tale. Tamsin has 24 of 24 hit points, AC 15, and all her slots. Pim is tying off the punt, and the path leads up to the village.

What does Tamsin do?

input.add_to_description: Day 1 of Tamsin's story: told Tamsin Vale his name was Pim, took two coppers for the lantern crossing, was impressed by her eye for rope. His dog is a big grey hound named Brannoc's-dog (the villagers call it Bran). Said Reedholm's people don't talk about the Isle to strangers, but Wren the healer will.

entries.text:
The man looks at the coppers, then at your hands on the pole, and something in his face eases. "Pim," he says. "Most who cross here can't tell tarred rope from wet string. Keep your coppers for the lantern, and welcome to the pole. Mind the stern, it pulls to the left."

The dog gets up on the doorstep, stretches, and trots down to the punt as if it had been invited. "That's Bran," Pim says. "He picks who rides."

You take the stern pole. The punt does pull left, as he said, and you correct it without thinking. The black water slides under the hull and the lantern throws a small gold circle on the reeds. Halfway over, Pim watches you work and says, "You've done this before." You say nothing, and he laughs once, shortly.

At the far bank he answers your question in pieces, tying off the rope with his eyes on the knot. The village is Reedholm, ten minutes along the bank. Everyone there knows about the Hollow Isle. They won't say much of it to strangers, because strangers come for the wrong reasons. A man came once to dig, and it did not end well for him. "The lights are in the old tales now," Pim says. "Nobody's seen them in years." He glances at you sidelong. "Funny you'd ask about a drowned stone. There is one, they say, on the Isle's west end, fallen over. But if you want the whole of it, don't ask me. Ask Wren, the healer. She keeps the village's memory, and she'll tell you what she thinks you've earned." He says the last part with a faint wince, like a man who has been tested himself.

He takes his two coppers and hands one back. "Rope-hand's rate. Go on. Mind her tongue."

It's five to six on Day 1 of your story. You're on the far bank with the ferry behind you. Ahead the yellow windows of Reedholm glow low among the reeds, twenty or so stilted houses joined by plank walks. A bell hangs at a post by the landing. Smoke rises from most of the chimneys, and a couple of children's voices carry across the water. You have full slots and 24 of 24 hit points.

What does Tamsin do?

I stop at the edge of the bank and look over the rope and the punt before I look at him. "Good rope. Whoever tars it knows the work." I dig two coppers out of my pouch and hold them out. "I'll take the lantern, and I'll pole if you want a second pair of hands. I was a ferrier myself, down south."

I ask, dry and unhurried, "What's the village across the water called, and is there anyone there who'd know about a drowned stone and lights over the water?"

entries.text:
Pim looks at the coppers, then at the pole in your hand, then at your hands. Ferriers look at hands first, and he sees yours are calloused where a pole's grip would wear them. Some of the wariness goes out of his shoulders, though not all of it.

"One copper's plenty. Lantern's free to anyone who knows to keep their feet off the net." He takes one coin and pushes the other back. "Pole if you like. She pulls to the left past the middle. The current's sly here."

You take the stern. He's right about the pull, and you correct for it before he can say so, which earns a short grunt that might be approval. The black water slides under the hull without a sound, and the dog pads aboard to sit between you like a passenger who has paid. The lights ahead aren't Reedholm itself, Pim says over his shoulder. They belong to the ford-end steading, six houses and a smokehouse. Reedholm is half a day on, along the raised bank, and bigger than it was. It's a landing now, with a market on the third day of the week.

When you ask about the stone and the lights, he stops hauling the rope for a moment. "Where'd you hear of that?" You tell him you didn't hear it, you dreamed it. He says nothing for several strokes. Then, flatly: "The Hollow Isle's a mile out from Reedholm's landing. There's a grey stone fallen at the west end, and you'll find it drowned at high water. The lights were there when I was a boy. They're gone now, mostly." He glances at the dark. "Mostly. Folk go out on the Isle by day, with salt and in numbers. Nobody pushes off alone after dusk, and you won't hear them say why."

On the far bank he ties off and nods at the road. "Ask for Wren at the Long House. She's the healer, and she'll want to know your business before she gives you a bed. She's good, and she's not kind about it." He pauses. "Brannoc's amulet hangs at her chest. Don't touch it, and don't ask her about it."

It's about six o'clock. Rain is still falling lightly, and you have a full set of slots and 24 hit points. The steading's lamps are warm yellow, and the road to Reedholm runs on into the dark. The dog has decided to walk with you as far as the first house.

What does Tamsin do?

The man looks at the coppers, then at your hands. They're a ferrier's hands, rope-scarred across the palms. Something in his face eases a little. "Pim," he says. "Pim Tarr. The rope's mine, and I tar it every spring. Nobody's said so in years." He takes one copper, not two, and waves off the pole. "Sit in the stern. You can tell me if I'm doing it wrong."

He isn't. The punt crosses on the rope with an easy hand-over-hand haul, and the dog, Bracken, rises at last and settles at your feet as if you'd been vouched for. The black water slides under the hull, and the lantern throws a small yellow circle on the reeds.

You ask your question, dry and unhurried. Pim goes quiet for three hauls of the rope. "Reedholm," he says. "Half a day on, along the bank. A landing town now, not a village. Eel-smokers, thatchers, a market on the fourth day." He doesn't look at you. "Drowned stone and lights. Who's been talking to you?"

You tell him nobody has. It was a dream. He nods slowly, as if that were worse. "There's a Hollow Isle a mile out from the landing. It has a fallen stone at the west end, and it's low enough that the water takes half of it in spring. Nobody cuts reeds there. When I was a boy there were lights over it, and a healer came and a good many people lived who shouldn't have. He didn't." He says no more of that. "If you want someone who knows the Isle, ask for Wren at the healing house. She wears a wooden amulet, and she'll look at you like you owe her money. Ask for Jory Rush at the staithe too, if the mist hasn't got him."

The punt grounds on the far bank with a soft knock. It is six in the evening, and the light is nearly gone. The track runs on into the reeds, and Reedholm is half a day away. Pim's hut on this side has a spare bench by the fire, if you wanted it.

Wren hears you out, her hand around the amulet. She is silent a moment, then shakes her head. "I don't know a name. I came up from Greywater as a girl, and the dead of this village are kept by the Rush family, not by me." She had the same thought you did, she says, and went through every post and rail in the Long House with a lamp a year ago, when the game started. The posts carry old notched tallies, but they are counts and carry no names. If there is a lost child, the village remembers her somewhere other than the wood.

She looks at you, and the flat look has changed a little. "Candle. A thing that wants a candle of its own. That's a better guess than mine." Then, harder: "Ode Rush keeps the burial tally in her house. She is up late, and she doesn't like being woken. She'll like less hearing there's a drowned thing under her hall. If you want a name, ask her tonight. Jory Rush would know the old stories too, since the children got the rhyme from him. His house is the one at the end of the north walk."

You climb to your feet and tell Wren what you think. She listens without moving, one hand around the amulet. She is quiet for a long moment, and then she says, "I don't know. But I know who would."

The old posts of the Long House are cut with names, she says, a custom older than the village. Wren carries the lamp out to the third post from the door, and you crouch beside her. Low down, where a child could have reached, a name has been scratched with a knife-point and weathered nearly smooth: LISE. Beneath it is a small knot, a child's good-luck knot, cut in the wood.

Wren's memory takes some finding (History, a 13, just enough). Lise was the headwoman's little sister, six years old. In the autumn flood, when Ode was a girl, Lise set a candle out on the west walk for their father's skiff coming home late. She went after it when the wind took it, and the water took her. They never found her. Ode is the last who remembers. She is old now, nearly seventy, and she lives in the end house on the landing. She hasn't spoken that name aloud in Wren's hearing in all the years she's known her.

"A candle that belongs to her," Wren says slowly. "Lit on land." She looks at you, and for the first time something other than testing is in her face. It might be grudging respect. "You'll want Ode awake for that. She won't thank either of us for it. Come on."

You climb to your feet and tell Wren what you think: that it isn't hunting the children, that it's looking for a light that was once its own. Wren is silent a while, and her hand stays on the amulet.

"A child of the village," she says. "Yes. I think you're right, and I've been afraid to say it." She tells you what she has. When she was new here, Ode Rush's old nurse told it as a bedtime story: a reed-cutter's small daughter, long before any of them, went out to meet her father's candle on the west walk in a gale, and the fen kept her. There was no body and no grave. The nurse thought her name was Lissa, or Tilly. She wasn't sure. "That's all I have, and it may be only a story."

You go looking for more. You take the lantern to the Long House posts and hunt for carved names, as the old cutters used to cut their marks. Investigation (4), a natural 1: the tide-lines have worn them smooth, and the one cut you think is a name turns out to be a knot in the wood. You learn nothing from the posts, and you rub your thumb raw on them for nothing.

Wren offers the next step herself. "Ode Rush is still alive. She's very old now, past seventy, and she lives in the stilt-house nearest the landing. She remembers what no one else does. She'll be awake. She never sleeps before midnight." She hesitates. "She will not like being asked about the west walk. Her husband went out on it the night he took the fever."

It's half past eight on a damp night. You have one 1st-level slot, two 2nd-level slots, and 24 of 24 hit points. The children sleep and the floor is quiet. Far out, one pale light waits.

You tell Wren what you think: that the voice wasn't hunting, that it was looking for a light that had once been its own. Wren says nothing for a long moment. Then she takes her lamp and walks you out along the west side of the hall, to the third stilt-post from the corner.

Low on the wood, where a child's hand would reach, a name is cut small and shallow: LISSA. Beside it is a single notch, the kind a cutter makes to mark a candle's place. The cuts are old and weathered nearly grey.

"Lissa Rush," Wren says. "I never knew her. Ode told me once, years back, and wouldn't say it twice. A cutter's girl, six or so, who went off the end of the west walk after a candle on a windy night. They dragged the channel for two days. The fen kept her. There's no grave, and no marker but this."

You try to read her face while she says it. Insight (7): you can't tell. She speaks evenly, and her hand is tight on the amulet, but whether that is old grief or something she hasn't said, you can't judge. She might be holding something back, or she might simply hate telling it.

"Ode is her father's brother's widow, or near enough," Wren adds. "She's old now and sleeps badly. She'd know whether the child had a favourite candle, a token, anything that was hers. I'd not wake her tonight. But I'd go to her at first light."

It's twenty past eight on a damp night. You have one 1st-level slot, two 2nd-level slots, and 24 of 24 hit points. The children sleep, the ferry-rope lies across the sill, and out west the far light waits.
